title: Trial endings that do not feel like a trap
metaTitle: Tell them before a free trial ends
excerpt: Say the end date before it arrives, name what stops, and show how to continue. A surprise lockout teaches people not to trust the next screen.
alt: Blue and orange ink blooming through water. The slow mix fits a piece about saying how a trial ends before the change arrives.
caption: The change should be visible before it arrives. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: When should you tell someone a free trial is ending?
faqs.answer: Tell them before the day it ends, inside the product, with a calendar date. A note about a week out and another a couple of days out is enough when both say the same date, the same losses, and the same way to continue. The ending screen should repeat those facts rather than introduce them for the first time.

faqs.question: What should a trial-end screen include?
faqs.answer: The date it ended, what still works, what has paused, and one clear way to continue or to export. If you delete data later, name that date on the same screen. A person should be able to act without opening a pricing page or a support chat.

faqs.question: Should a trial make people contact support in order to stop?
faqs.answer: Let them stop in the product, then confirm what they keep and how long the archive remains. A required chat, a hidden setting, or a survey that blocks the export teaches people to dispute the charge and to skip the next product that asks for a card. One optional question after the door is open is plenty.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
A free trial ending ux is three sentences the buyer can repeat a week before the lock: the date, what stops, and how to continue. Say them in the product before the day arrives. A surprise lockout teaches the buyer not to trust the next screen, including the one that asks them to pay.

The rest of the interface can be careful and still lose that trust in one morning. Write the ending as part of the product, in the same voice as the welcome. The billing system can enforce the date. It should not be the first place the date appears.

## What the ending has to say

Three facts, in a fixed order.

The date. A calendar day, not "soon," and not "when your trial expires" with the day left off. If the product is used across timezones, name the zone you are counting in. A founder in one city and a teammate in another should not disagree about whether the trial is still open.

What stops. Features, seats, shared links, and whether the account becomes read-only. Use the names people see in the navigation. "Advanced reports" is useless if the screen they rely on is called Weekly board.

How to continue. The plan that matches how they have been working, and the button that does the thing. If two plans are honest options, give each one line of difference. A pricing page with six cards is a second product. The ending screen can link to it after the choice is clear.

Write these three as sentences you could paste into a release note. If you cannot, the timer is running on a policy you have not written yet.

## Say the date before it arrives

The person who invited a colleague on Thursday should not learn on Monday that the invite no longer works. Pick a rhythm and keep it. A note inside the product about seven days out, another about two days out, and a final one the morning of. Email can carry the same sentences. The in-product note is the one they will believe, because it sits where the work is.

Nielsen Norman Group's [research on how long people stay on web pages](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) is a constraint on how those notes are written. Jakob Nielsen reported that users often leave a web page in 10 to 20 seconds, and that you have to communicate the value of the page within about 10 seconds if you want longer attention. A reminder that opens with thanks, a logo, and a paragraph of brand warmth will lose the people who needed the date. Put the date in the first line. Put what stops in the second. Put the action in the third.

That research also found that the average page visit lasts a little less than a minute, and that people have time to read only about a quarter of the text on pages they actually open. Your reminder is a label with a next step. It is not a letter from the founder.

Do not decorate the date. The date is already specific. A flashing countdown, or a subject line that sounds like a collection notice, spends the trust you needed for the renewal itself. State the day. Stop.

Who receives it matters as much as the wording. The admin who can pay should get the note. Members who will feel the lock should get a shorter version that tells them who can continue the account, so they do not all write to support with the same question. If only one address is on the billing profile, say so in the product, where the rest of the team can see it.

## What stops, in the customer's words

Split the change into three buckets, and say all three. Silence on any bucket will be filled in with the harsher guess.

What they keep. Login, history, and the export that still runs. People stay calmer when the first sentence is what remains. If shared read-only links keep working, say that. If they die at midnight, say that too, because someone has probably pasted the link into a doc their customer uses.

What pauses. The features that freeze until they continue. Say whether paused work is still visible. A board they can see and not edit is a different product from a board that vanishes. Name which one you built.

What is removed, and on what later date. If you delete projects after a grace period, the grace period is part of the ending. Put it in the same sequence as the trial date, not in a terms page linked from the footer. If you do not delete anything, say that in the same plain voice. People assume deletion when you do not mention the archive.

Seat changes need the same honesty. If the trial included five seats and the continued plan includes three, say which seats remain and that an admin chooses. Do not silently drop the last two people who joined.

## How to continue, on the same screen

The continue path sits beside the facts. One primary action. If they have already added a card, the button can confirm the plan and the next charge date. If they have not, the button takes them to that step without a tour of the marketing site.

Say what the button will do before they press it. "Continue on the Team plan. The first charge is on the day the trial ends." If the charge is immediate because they waited until the last morning, say immediate. A person who thought they had a day left will dispute a charge they did not expect, and they will be right to feel misled even if a tooltip somewhere mentioned it.

Payment failure is a different event from a trial that ended. A card that declines should not reuse the "trial over" layout. Say the charge failed, what still works today, and how to try another card. Mixing those stories trains the team to describe every billing problem as a trap.

If a human has to approve the switch, name the wait in language you can keep. "We reply on the next business day" is a policy you can staff. "Instant" is a claim you should make only when the charge and the unlock happen in the same step. Do not borrow the word from a payment provider's happy path if your own review sits in between.

Early upgrades should use the same sentences. Someone who continues on day four should see the new end date, what they now have, and that the trial clock has stopped. Leave the trial-end sequence for people who are still on the trial. Sending "your trial is ending" to a paying account is how a careful product starts to sound automatic.

## The lock that teaches distrust

Let them stop. Tell them what they keep and what they lose. Confirm the stop in the same voice you used for the welcome.

A maze is a reason to dispute the charge and a reason not to come back. If ending the trial means a hunt through settings, a chat widget, and a required essay about why they are leaving, you have built a trap. Some people will pay because leaving is harder. They will remember the hunt the next time a product asks for a card.

The ending screen can ask one optional question. It should not block the export, the confirmation, or the door. A survey that gates the archive is the maze in a quieter color.

The lock screen itself should be dull and specific. "Your trial ended on 4 May. You can still export projects until 18 May. Continue on the Team plan, or download the archive." Skip the illustration of a locked gate. Skip the line that tells them they will miss you. The useful content is the date, the remaining access, and the two actions.

Read this screen against the notes you sent earlier. If the grace period on the lock screen is shorter than the one in the seven-day note, you have two policies. Ship one.

Admins need a record. They should be able to see who was told and on what day. A founder who learns about the end from a teammate's screenshot has already lost the thread, and support will hear the story secondhand.

## A review before the timer ships

Read the sequence out loud as the buyer, with the inbox closed, using only the product.

- A week out: can you state the date, what stops, and how to continue without scrolling past a hero?
- Two days out: are you repeating those facts, or introducing a new penalty?
- The morning of: does the product match the email word for word on the date and the grace period?
- The day after: is the blocked state explained, and is export where you said it would be?
- A week later: if they return, is the door the same door?

Ask someone who did not design the flow to find the end date from inside the app. If they open settings, billing, a help drawer, and then give up, the date is not in the product yet. Put it where the work is, in a banner or a panel the admin already passes.

Check the empty states that appear after the lock. A button that still says Create, and then fails, feels broken. Replace it with the sentence from the ending screen. The interface should have one explanation, reused, until the account continues or the archive window closes.

## Where this sits in the product

Trial endings are specified with the rest of the interface. The screen, the shorter note to members, and the admin record belong in the same pass. A billing portal's default email is a fallback, not the design.

The next failure, if the trial itself was honest, is often the moment someone brings old work in. [Import flows for a tool people already use](/blog/import-flows-for-a-tool-people-already-use) is the piece to read next, because a quiet failed import will be blamed on the whole product the same way a surprise lock is.
